title: LAPSUS$
summary: LAPSUS$ is the public label for a loosely organised, English speaking intrusion group whose tradecraft de-emphasises malware in favour of human manipulation. Reporting describes recruitment of insiders and help desk staff, payment for access, SIM swapping to intercept one time codes, repeated push notifications to exhaust a user into approving a login, and heavy use of remote access already granted to contractors and vendors. Once inside, the group prioritises source code, customer data and collaboration platforms, then leaks or threatens to leak the material instead of encrypting it. Defender visible evidence is therefore mostly identity based: impossible travel, new multi factor authentication device registrations, help desk password resets without a verified request, session token replay, and bulk download from cloud storage by a legitimate looking account. The common misunderstanding is that a group without sophisticated malware is a nuisance: identity is the control plane of modern enterprises, and an operator who lives entirely in it can reach far more data than a malware drop would. Attribution is complicated by the loose membership and by imitation, and public reporting notes that some participants have been identified and prosecuted.

beginner.definition: LAPSUS$ is a name for a group of young attackers known for tricking people rather than breaking software. They call help desks, send messages to staff and try to buy access from insiders. Their goal is usually to steal data and then threaten to publish it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many companies trust their login systems and multi factor codes, and this group attacks exactly that trust. They do not need a clever virus if a tired employee approves a login prompt at midnight. Leaked source code or customer records can damage a company for years, and paying the group does not guarantee silence. Because the attackers often sound like real staff, your help desk procedures are part of your security, not just customer service.
howItWorks: The group studies a company on social media and learns who works there and who supports them.
They call the help desk pretending to be an employee who has lost a phone.
They ask for a password reset or a new multi factor code, using details they have collected.
They also send repeated login approvals, hoping a tired person finally clicks accept.
Once inside, they join internal chat channels and watch conversations to learn the systems.
They download source code and customer data, then demand payment to keep it private.
beginner.example: Think of an office building with a very strong front door and a friendly receptionist. You cannot pick the lock, so instead you learn the receptionist's name, mention a shared project, and say you forgot your badge. She checks the visitor list, sees your name, and lets you in. No lock was broken. The attack used the rules of the building as the way in. LAPSUS$ works exactly like that visitor. It attacks the polite procedures that let real people back into their accounts.
takeaways: Verify identity before any password reset, using a second method the caller cannot control.
Multi factor prompts that arrive without you logging in should be denied and reported.
Watch for new device registrations and bulk cloud downloads, not just unusual files.

objectives: Explain how help desk impersonation and multi factor fatigue attacks bypass authentication controls without malware.
Identify the identity telemetry that reveals this style of intrusion, including device registration and session anomalies.
Describe the risks of insider recruitment and why third party and contractor access must be governed.
Assess extortion through data leak threats and explain why payment does not resolve the exposure.
Outline help desk verification procedures that resist social engineering without harming legitimate users.
